content.summary:
## Overview

This section covers how objects move between Amazon S3 storage classes and how Lifecycle Rules automate transitions, expiration, version cleanup and multipart-upload cleanup, filtered by prefix or tag. It also covers S3 Storage Class Analysis, the reporting tool that recommends when to move data to Standard IA. For SAA-C03 this is core Cost-Optimized storage design (managing S3 object lifecycles, storage tiering, selecting the data lifecycle), so expect scenario questions that give retention windows and retrieval-time requirements and ask you to pick storage classes plus a lifecycle design.

## Core Concepts

- **Storage class transition:** Moving an object from one S3 storage class to another (for example Standard to Standard IA to Glacier) without changing its key; can be automated with Lifecycle Rules.
- **Standard IA:** The target class for infrequently accessed objects that must still be retrieved quickly; the storage class S3 Analytics makes recommendations about (together with Standard).
- **Glacier / Glacier Deep Archive:** Archive classes for objects you do not need fast access to; Deep Archive is the deeper, cheaper archive tier used after a shorter-term archive step in the section's scenarios.
- **Lifecycle Rule transition action:** A rule action that moves objects to another storage class after a condition such as days since creation (e.g. move to Standard IA at 60 days, to Glacier after 6 months).
- **Lifecycle Rule expiration action:** A rule action that deletes (expires) objects after some time, e.g. deleting access log files after 365 days.
- **Noncurrent version deletion:** An expiration action that deletes old versions of an object when versioning is enabled.
- **Incomplete multipart upload cleanup:** An expiration action that deletes incomplete Multi-Part uploads, avoiding storage charges for unfinished uploads.
- **Prefix filter:** A lifecycle rule scoped to a key prefix, e.g. s3://mybucket/mp3/* so only that folder of objects is affected.
- **Tag filter:** A lifecycle rule scoped to object tags, e.g. Department: Finance, so rules follow business meaning rather than key path.
- **S3 Storage Class Analysis:** An S3 Analytics feature that monitors access patterns and produces a daily .csv report (storage class by object age) to help decide when to transition objects.

## Key Comparisons

- **Standard IA vs One-Zone IA:** Both are for infrequently accessed data, but the section's thumbnail scenario uses One-Zone IA for easily recreated objects, so pick it when the data can be regenerated and Standard IA otherwise.
- **Glacier vs Glacier Deep Archive:** Deep Archive is the deeper archive step used after an earlier Glacier-class or Standard IA stage when the retrieval requirement is looser (hours rather than immediate).
- **Transition action vs Expiration action:** Transition changes the storage class of an object that stays alive; expiration deletes the object (or old versions / incomplete uploads).
- **Prefix filter vs Tag filter:** Prefix scopes by key path (s3://mybucket/mp3/*); tag scopes by object metadata (Department: Finance), which is better when the rule must follow objects regardless of key layout.
- **S3 Storage Class Analysis vs Lifecycle Rules:** Analysis only observes and reports on access patterns (recommendations for Standard and Standard IA only); Lifecycle Rules are what actually perform transitions and expirations.
- **Versioning vs Lifecycle expiration:** With versioning enabled a delete is hidden by a delete marker, so old data is removed by expiring noncurrent versions, not by ordinary object expiration.

## Common Misunderstandings

- S3 Storage Class Analysis performs transitions for you — it does not; it produces recommendations that you then implement as Lifecycle Rules.
- S3 Analytics can recommend Glacier transitions — it only covers Standard and Standard IA and does not work for One-Zone IA or Glacier.
- Turning on versioning is enough to clean up old data — you must also expire noncurrent versions, or they keep accruing cost.
- Deleting an object in a versioned bucket removes the data — it adds a delete marker; the object versions persist until noncurrent-version expiration.
- Lifecycle rules can only target a whole bucket — they can be scoped by prefix or by object tag.
- S3 Analytics gives instant results — allow 24 to 48 hours before analysis appears, and the report is updated daily.

## Mental Models

- Think of Lifecycle Rules as a conveyor belt: whenever an age/condition is met, an object moves to the next class or falls off (expire).
- Think of S3 Storage Class Analysis as an X-ray of the bucket that tells you where to place the belt; the belt itself is the Lifecycle Rule.
- Think of a delete marker as a curtain in front of the object: versioning keeps the object behind the curtain, and noncurrent-version expiration finally removes it.
- Think of a prefix as a folder address and a tag as a label on the parcel — either can steer the rule.

## Exceptions & Edge Cases

- Noncurrent version transitions/deletion only exist if versioning is enabled.
- Incomplete multipart uploads consume storage until a rule expires them; clean them up explicitly.
- Objects can be transitioned multiple times in sequence (Standard → Standard IA → Glacier Deep Archive) as in Scenario 2.
- Lifecycle rules by tag require the tag to exist on the object to be matched.
- An object can be both transitioned and expired by the same overall configuration when requirements differ per object set (source images vs thumbnails in Scenario 1).

## When to Use Which

- Objects are accessed rarely but must still be retrievable quickly. → **Transition to Standard IA.**
- Archive data that does not need fast access. → **Transition to Glacier or Glacier Deep Archive.**
- Log files older than 365 days are no longer needed. → **Expiration action to delete access log files after 365 days.**
- Versioned bucket accumulating old object versions. → **Expire noncurrent versions.**
- Bucket has many abandoned multipart uploads. → **Expiration action to delete incomplete multipart uploads.**
- Only one application path's objects should be tiered. → **Rule scoped to a prefix (s3://mybucket/mp3/*).**
- Rules must follow objects across arbitrary key layouts, e.g. by department. → **Rule scoped to a tag (Department: Finance).**
- You don't know which objects are cold and want data-driven lifecycle design. → **Start with S3 Storage Class Analysis, then build Lifecycle Rules from its report.**
- Objects can be regenerated easily and are only needed 60 days. → **Store in One-Zone IA and expire after 60 days.**

## Patterns to Recognize

- "immediately retrievable for 60 days, then up to 6 hours" → **Standard (or Standard IA) for the immediate window, transition to Glacier afterwards.**
- "thumbnails can be easily recreated" → **One-Zone IA plus expiration.**
- "recover deleted objects immediately for 30 days, within 48 hours for up to 365 days" → **Versioning + noncurrent version transitions (Standard IA then Glacier Deep Archive).**
- "which service recommends when to transition objects" → **S3 Storage Class Analysis.**
- "old versions" or "incomplete multipart uploads" → **Expiration actions in a lifecycle rule.**
- "only Finance department files" → **Tag-based lifecycle rule.**
- "only files under the mp3 folder" → **Prefix-based lifecycle rule.**

## Exam Traps

- “S3 Analytics can be used for One-Zone IA and Glacier optimization.” — Analysis recommendations cover only Standard and Standard IA; it does not work for One-Zone IA or Glacier.
- “Enabling versioning automatically deletes old versions.” — Versioning retains versions; you must add noncurrent-version expiration/transition actions.
- “Lifecycle rules are a substitute for S3 Analytics.” — They are complementary: Analytics informs the rules, the rules execute them.
- “Delete markers free the storage of overwritten objects.” — Only expiring noncurrent versions removes the underlying versions.
- “Lifecycle rules cannot be targeted narrowly.” — They can be filtered by prefix or by object tag.
- “S3 Analytics produces data immediately.” — It takes 24 to 48 hours to start seeing analysis, with daily report updates.

## Beyond the Source (tutor knowledge)

- Current S3 lifecycle configurations often distinguish current-version and noncurrent-version actions explicitly (transition and expiration for each), which is consistent with the section's noncurrent-version scenarios.
- Lifecycle rules support minimum object-age thresholds in whole days and are evaluated asynchronously, so transitions are not instantaneous at the exact day boundary; the exam generally tests the intended design rather than timing exactness.

Transition actions and expiration actions are separate rule actions; a rule may have both.
Expiration actions can delete: current objects after N days, noncurrent (old) versions when versioning is enabled, and incomplete Multi-Part uploads.
Rules can filter by prefix (e.g. s3://mybucket/mp3/*) or by object tag (e.g. Department: Finance).
S3 Storage Class Analysis gives recommendations only for Standard and Standard IA.
S3 Analytics does NOT work for One-Zone IA or Glacier.
S3 Analytics report is updated daily; it takes 24 to 48 hours to start seeing data analysis.
S3 Analytics is a good first step to build or improve Lifecycle Rules — it is not an automation of transitions itself.

quiz.question: A media company uploads source images to S3. The images must be instantly retrievable for 60 days after upload; after that, retrieval within a few hours is acceptable. Archival cost matters. Which lifecycle design fits?
options: Store in Standard, then use a lifecycle rule to transition to Glacier after 60 days
Store in Standard IA, then use a lifecycle rule to expire the objects after 60 days
Store in One-Zone IA, then use a lifecycle rule to transition to Deep Archive after 60 days
Store in Glacier Instant Retrieval and transition to Standard after 60 days
quiz.explanation: Standard gives immediate retrieval during the 60-day window and a transition to Glacier at day 60 matches the loosened hours-level retrieval need. Standard IA plus expiration deletes data the company must still keep. One-Zone IA is for easily recreated data, and Deep Archive is normally a later step after a shorter archive tier in this section's designs. Glacier Instant Retrieval is not the right first tier for data needing immediate access at creation.

quiz.question: An application on EC2 generates image thumbnails that can be regenerated at any time and only need to be kept for 60 days. Which configuration is most cost-appropriate?
options: Store thumbnails in Standard with a lifecycle rule to transition to Glacier Deep Archive after 60 days
Store thumbnails in One-Zone IA with a lifecycle rule to expire them after 60 days
Store thumbnails in Standard IA with a lifecycle rule to delete noncurrent versions after 60 days
Store thumbnails in Glacier Flexible Retrieval with a lifecycle rule to transition to Standard IA after 60 days
quiz.explanation: One-Zone IA suits infrequently accessed data that is easily recreated, and an expiration action deletes it at day 60. Transitioning regenerable thumbnails to Deep Archive keeps charges alive past the 60-day requirement. Noncurrent version deletion only applies to old versions in a versioned bucket, not the current thumbnails. Storing in Glacier and later transitioning back to Standard IA is backwards and keeps data you intended to expire.

quiz.question: Objects are infrequently accessed but must still be retrieved quickly when requested, and the data is not easily reproducible. Which storage class is the appropriate lifecycle transition target?
options: Glacier Deep Archive
One-Zone IA
Standard IA
Glacier Flexible Retrieval
quiz.explanation: Standard IA is the section's target for infrequently accessed objects that still need fast retrieval. Deep Archive and Glacier Flexible Retrieval are archive tiers for data without fast-access needs. One-Zone IA also serves infrequent access but is chosen for objects that can be easily recreated, which does not match this requirement.

quiz.question: A company needs deleted S3 objects recoverable immediately for 30 days and, after that, recoverable within 48 hours for up to 365 days. How should the storage classes be sequenced?
options: Transition current versions to Standard IA at 30 days and expire the bucket at 365 days
Transition noncurrent versions to Glacier Deep Archive at 30 days, then to Standard IA at 365 days
Enable versioning and expire noncurrent versions immediately on deletion
Enable versioning, transition noncurrent versions to Standard IA, then transition them to Glacier Deep Archive
quiz.explanation: Versioning keeps deleted objects behind a delete marker, and the noncurrent versions can be moved from Standard IA to Glacier Deep Archive as the 48-hour recovery requirement takes over. Expiring the bucket at 365 days removes objects the rule says must be recoverable. Moving noncurrent versions first to Deep Archive and later to Standard IA reverses the retrieval-time progression. Expiring noncurrent versions immediately destroys the ability to recover deleted objects at all.

quiz.question: A versioned bucket's storage cost keeps rising because overwritten objects remain. Which lifecycle action removes them?
options: An expiration action that deletes noncurrent versions
An expiration action that deletes incomplete multipart uploads
A transition action that moves the objects to Standard IA
An expiration action that deletes the current object after 30 days
quiz.explanation: Noncurrent version expiration is the action that removes the old versions kept by versioning. Expiring incomplete multipart uploads only cleans up unfinished uploads. A transition to Standard IA changes the storage class of retained versions but does not delete them. Expiring current objects adds delete markers and leaves the underlying versions, and so does not reduce cost.

quiz.question: A bucket receives multi-part uploads that applications frequently abandon before completion, and storage charges are growing. What should you add to the lifecycle configuration?
options: A transition of incomplete uploads to One-Zone IA after 7 days
A transition of incomplete uploads to Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days
An expiration action to delete incomplete multipart uploads
An expiration action on noncurrent versions after 7 days
quiz.explanation: Expiring incomplete multipart uploads removes the parts that are charged while an upload never completes. Transitioning incomplete uploads assumes partial uploads can be tiered like objects, which does not match the section's cleanup mechanism. Noncurrent version expiration applies only to old object versions in a versioned bucket, which is unrelated to unfinished uploads.

quiz.question: Finance department files must follow a lifecycle rule even though teams can upload them under any key path. Other departments' objects must not be affected. Which filter satisfies this?
options: A rule scoped to the prefix s3://mybucket/finance/*
A rule scoped to the object tag Department: Finance
A bucket policy that restricts lifecycle rules to Finance IAM roles
A rule scoped to the prefix s3://mybucket/*, applied to the whole bucket
quiz.explanation: Tag-based rules follow the object's metadata regardless of key layout, and only tagged Finance objects match. A prefix rule only works if every Finance object reliably lands under that path, which the requirement rules out. A bucket policy controls access, not lifecycle scope. A whole-bucket rule affects all departments, violating the constraint.

quiz.question: A team wants to know which objects are cold and when they should move to Standard IA, but has no data on access patterns yet. What should they do first?
options: Create a lifecycle rule that transitions all objects to Standard IA after 30 days
Enable S3 Storage Class Analysis to collect access patterns and produce reports
Create a lifecycle rule that expires objects after 30 days
Enable versioning so old objects become noncurrent versions
quiz.explanation: Storage Class Analysis observes access patterns and produces a daily report that forms the basis for building lifecycle rules. Transitioning everything after 30 days is a guess made without the data the team lacks. Expiring objects does not inform tiering decisions and risks data loss. Versioning retains old versions but says nothing about which objects are cold.

quiz.question: Which statement about S3 Storage Class Analysis is correct?
options: It gives recommendations for One-Zone IA and Glacier as well as Standard IA
It performs the storage class transitions automatically once enabled
It takes 24 to 48 hours before analysis appears, and the report is updated daily
It produces recommendations only for Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive
quiz.explanation: Analysis takes 24 to 48 hours to begin showing data, and the report refreshes daily. Analysis recommendations cover Standard and Standard IA only and do not work for One-Zone IA or Glacier. Analysis never executes transitions; lifecycle rules do that. Limiting recommendations to Glacier classes misstates which classes are covered.

quiz.question: Why should lifecycle configuration include both transition actions and expiration actions rather than choosing one type?
options: Transitions move objects to cheaper classes over time, and expirations delete data that is no longer needed
Transitions delete old versions, and expirations move current objects between storage classes
Expiration actions are required before any transition action can be evaluated
Transitions and expirations can never be combined in a single lifecycle configuration
quiz.explanation: Transition actions handle tiering so live objects cost less, while expiration actions remove objects, noncurrent versions and incomplete uploads that no longer need to exist. Deletion belongs to expiration actions, not transitions. No rule requires an expiration before a transition is evaluated. Rules may contain both action types, and one configuration can serve different object sets.

sections.objective: Choose between native S3 event notifications and EventBridge for event-driven integration, and identify the IAM permissions and authentication constraints each option requires.
sections.text:
[Page 300]
S3 	– 	Requester Pays
• 	In general, bucket owners pay for all
Amazon S3 storage and data transfer
costs associated with their bucket
• 	With Requester Pays buckets, the
requester instead of the bucket owner

sections.title: S3 Performance: Baseline Throughput, Multi-Part Upload, Transfer Acceleration, Byte-Range Fetches
sections.objective: Select S3 performance features and prefix strategies that meet a stated throughput, upload speed, or download resilience requirement.
sections.text:
[Page 304]
S3 	– 	Baseline Performance
• 	Amazon S3 automatically scales to high request rates, latency 100-200 ms
• 	Your application can achieve at least 	3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE or
5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per prefix in a bucket.
• 	There are no limits to the number of prefixes in a bucket.
• 	Example (object path => prefix):
• 	bucket/folder1/sub1/file => /folder1/sub1/
• 	bucket/folder1/sub2/file => /folder1/sub2/
• 	bucket/1/file 	=> /1/
• 	bucket/2/file 	=> /2/
• 	If you spread reads across all four prefixes evenly, you can achieve 22,000
requests per second for GET and HEAD

[Page 305]
S3 Performance
• 	Multi-Part upload:
• 	recommended for files > 100MB,
must use for files > 5GB
• 	Can help parallelize uploads (speed
up transfers)
• 	S3 Transfer Acceleration
• 	Increase transfer speed by transferring
file to an AWS edge location which will
forward the data to the S3 bucket in the
target region
• 	Compatible with multi-part upload

S3 Batch Operations
• 	Perform bulk operations on existing S3 objects with a
single request, example:
• 	Modify object metadata & properties
• 	Copy objects between S3 buckets
• 	Encrypt un-encrypted objects
• 	Modify ACLs, tags
• 	Restore objects from S3 Glacier
• 	Invoke Lambda function to perform custom action on
each object
• 	A job consists of a list of objects, the action to
perform, and optional parameters
• 	S3 Batch Operations manages retries, tracks progress,
sends completion notifications, generate reports …
• 	You can use S3 Inventory to get object list and use
